item.title: Prasad Trial: Evidence Under Fire
item.description: The hearing into the admissibility of a company document in the trial of former deputy prime minister Professor Biman Prasad continues at 3.30pm today. The matter was heard before Magistrate Yogesh Prasad, with the defence arguing that the document was hearsay and should not be admitted unless the prosecution could establish a recognised exception to the hearsay rule.
item.content:encoded:
The hearing into the admissibility of a company document in the trial of former deputy prime minister Professor Biman Prasad continues at 3.30pm today.

The matter was heard before Magistrate Yogesh Prasad, with the defence arguing that the document was hearsay and should not be admitted unless the prosecution could establish a recognised exception to the hearsay rule.

Defence lawyer Richard Naidu submitted that the document, relating to the particulars of directors and officers of a company, had been produced through a witness who was not its maker and could not establish the truth or accuracy of the information contained in it.

Mr Naidu argued that the fact the document was a statutory return required under the former Companies Act and filed with the Registrar of Companies did not, by itself, make its contents admissible or conclusive evidence.

The defence also disputed the prosecution’s reliance on the document being a public record, submitting that there was no general hearsay exception providing that a document simply became admissible because it had been filed with a public authority.

Mr Naidu referred Magistrate Prasad to provisions of the former Companies Act concerning certificates of incorporation and registration, arguing that where Parliament intended a document to constitute conclusive evidence, the legislation expressly said so.

The defence submitted that such provisions did not extend to the disputed company return, and that the prosecution had not produced authority establishing that the document was admissible as an exception to the hearsay rule. Mr Naidu also relied on the constitutional right of an accused person to challenge evidence presented against them, arguing that admitting the document without its maker being available for cross-examination would prejudice Prof Prasad’s ability to challenge its contents.

The prosecution had earlier argued that the document was a statutory return and formed part of the records maintained by the Registrar of Companies.

It submitted that the document was prepared and filed pursuant to statutory requirements under Section 202 of the former Companies Act and was therefore part of the statutory record-keeping system.

The prosecution also referred to the Public Records Act and a previous High Court decision concerning company records, arguing that the document qualified for admission.

The defence rejected that argument, saying the previous case was a civil matter and did not establish a hearsay exception in criminal proceedings.

item.title: Industry body pushes for international recognised spa qualifications
item.description: THE Fiji Hotel and Tourism Association is looking to strengthen standards across the tourism industry by introducing internationally recognised qualifications in beauty, wellness and spa services. Association chief executive Fantasha Lockington said the initiative aligned with the industry’s broader work to introduce sustainability standards across tourism operations.
item.content:encoded:
THE Fiji Hotel and Tourism Association is looking to strengthen standards across the tourism industry by introducing internationally recognised qualifications in beauty, wellness and spa services.

Association chief executive Fantasha Lockington said the initiative aligned with the industry’s broader work to introduce sustainability standards across tourism operations.

She made the remarks at the CIDESCO Fiji Congress 2026 in Nadi on Monday.

She said sustainability was being considered across every aspect of tourism, from accommodation and tours to recycling and environmental management.

“At the hotel and tourism association, currently we are working to introduce sustainability standards into every element of tourism operations,” Ms Lockington said.

She said pursuing CIDESCO qualifications was a natural next step because the organisation provided internationally recognised standards for skills, safety and professionalism.

Ms Lockington said internationally recognised qualifications would give tourists, investors and tourism operators greater confidence in the quality of services provided in Fiji.

“If we can give our guests, our investors and our operators confidence in the standard of care that we’re giving and that our guests are receiving, I think that’s a very, very natural step for us to be taking.

She said health and safety were particularly important in the wellness and spa industry because treatments often involved close personal contact.

Ms Lockington said maintaining high safety standards was important to Fiji’s reputation as a tourism destination.

She also called for the development of wellness standards that incorporated Pacific and Fijian traditions while remaining aligned with globally recognised certification.

“I think that those are natural things that you sit together.”

She said traditional elements such as the Fijian approach to touch, connection, oils and healing could complement international standards.

The aim, she said, should not be to replace global standards but to build on them while creating a distinctive Fijian offering.

Ms Lockington said this would also provide local therapists with greater opportunities for professional recognition and career mobility.

“Not just about replacing or embracing global standards, but about adding to them and giving our therapists a pathway to career mobility and recognition that is rooted in something that is authentically Fijian.”

The CIDESCO Congress is the leading global gathering for beauty, wellness, and spa therapy professionals, organised by Switzerland based CIDESCO (Comité International d’Esthétique et de Cosmétologie) International.

item.title: $16m in mature policies in 8 months | 62,000 policies strong as life insurance provider turns 70
item.description: LIFE insurance service provider Life Insurance Corporation of India (LICI) Fiji has so far paid out 970 mature policies valued at $16.63 million up until August month-end this year. The Fiji Times obtained these statistics yesterday as the organisation marks its 70th anniversary of operations in the country.
item.content:encoded:
LIFE insurance service provider Life Insurance Corporation of India (LICI) Fiji has so far paid out 970 mature policies valued at $16.63 million up until August month-end this year.

The Fiji Times obtained these statistics yesterday as the organisation marks its 70th anniversary of operations in the country.

Also, between January 1-August 31 this year, LICI Fiji has settled 124 death claims valued at $3.06m and 3666 survival benefit claims worth $12.30m.

Last year, the institution paid out a total of $47.55m across 6999 claims, comprising: $4.74m paid across 177 death claims, $18.90m paid across 5619 survival benefit claims, and $23.91m paid across 1203 mature policies.

In a presentation to the media yesterday, LICI Fiji general manager Shridhar Pathare also highlighted the company’s financial standing as at December 31 last year.

Total assets increased by 4.15 per cent over the year to $1.05 billion; net insurance premiums increased to $83.6m from $78.9m the prior year; surplus totalled $27.29m – of which $25.92m was added to the policyholders’ account as accumulated bonus; solvency surplus of $288.8m – in excess of its minimum required solvency margin of $86.9m; more than 62,000 policies serviced; and more than 15,000 policyholders also availed the facility of loan under their policies with a total of $52.10m paid out.

“Seventy years is more than a milestone, it’s a testament to the trust that generations of Fijian families have placed in us,” Mr Pathare said.

“From our first policy issued in 1956 to the policyholders’ funds of over $1b we now hold in trust, our purpose has remained the same – to give the people of Fiji the confidence to plan for tomorrow, no matter what life brings.”

Mr Pathare said they had planned a series of initiatives for its policyholders and the wider community to mark this anniversary.

“As we look ahead, our focus is on continuing to strengthen our financial position while staying true t what has always set us apart – genuine care for the people we serve.”

Today, LICI Fiji has 36 employees serving from four offices in Suva, Lautoka, Nadi and Labasa; and 211 agents spread across the country. Its product basket comprises 16 plans open for sale, including endowment, money-back endowment plan, and whole life and group plans.

item.title: Lower court to hear arguments
item.description: THE Suva Magistrate’s Court will today hear crucial arguments on whether key corporate records can be admitted as evidence in the trial of former deputy prime minister Professor Biman Prasad. His lawyer Richard Naidu objected to one particular document, which contains details of the directors of Platinum Hotels & Resorts PTE Ltd, which was registered on December 4, 2015.
item.content:encoded:
THE Suva Magistrate’s Court will today hear crucial arguments on whether key corporate records can be admitted as evidence in the trial of former deputy prime minister Professor Biman Prasad.

His lawyer Richard Naidu objected to one particular document, which contains details of the directors of Platinum Hotels & Resorts PTE Ltd, which was registered on December 4, 2015.

The prosecution yesterday called Manase Talemaipapalagi, the executive officer at the Registrar of Companies, who identified the document and told the court that it showed Prof Prasad was one of three directors at that time.

Mr Naidu argued that the document was provided to the Registrar of Companies and was not an official document created by the registrar and was therefore hearsay.

He submitted that it could not be relied on to prove the truth of its contents because the person who supplied or signed the information had not been called to give evidence.

FICAC’s acting manager Legal Joseph Work, opposed the objection, arguing that the document was relevant and related directly to the directorship of Platinum Hotels and Resorts. Mr Work also raised the possibility that the document could be admitted as a business record under the Evidence Act.

The matter resumes at 11.30am for arguments on the objection.

Prof Prasad faces charges of failing to comply with statutory disclosure requirements and providing false information in a statutory declaration.

FICAC alleges he failed to disclose his directorship in Platinum Hotels & Resorts PTE Ltd in his declaration of assets, liabilities, and income as of December 31, 2015.

item.title: Samuela Tawase released under compulsory community treatment order
item.description: Samuela Tawase, acquitted in May on a charge of sacrilege relating to the Samabula Shiv Temple, has been released into the community under a compulsory community treatment order. Mr Tawase was accused of attacking the Samabula Hindu temple in July last year.
item.content:encoded:
Samuela Tawase, acquitted in May on a charge of sacrilege relating to the Samabula Shiv Temple, has been released into the community under a compulsory community treatment order.

Mr Tawase was accused of attacking the Samabula Hindu temple in July last year.

He was acquitted in May after the court found that he was of unsound mind at the time of the alleged offending.

The matter was before Magistrate Yogesh Prasad, who heard evidence from a doctor about Mr Tawase’s mental health and ongoing treatment.

The court heard Mr Tawase had been receiving treatment at Saint Giles Hospital and would require continued medication and monitoring if released into the community.

The doctor told the court Mr Tawase would need to take medication every night and receive a monthly injection as part of his treatment.

The court also heard there was a high risk of relapse if Mr Tawase resumed substance abuse or stopped taking his medication, which could result in a deterioration of his mental health and potentially further offending.

Mr Tawase is to be placed under a compulsory community treatment order, requiring him to attend monthly clinical reviews and continue his prescribed medication and injections.

His family will be responsible for supervising his daily medication and must report to the relevant authorities if he stops taking his medication, fails to attend treatment or resumes using drugs.

The court also ordered that Mr Tawase must not consume drugs, including marijuana, or alcohol.

Magistrate Prasad said the compulsory community treatment would provide Mr Tawase with an opportunity to rehabilitate in the community while ensuring he continued to receive medical treatment and family support.

item.title: Efforts to preserve, promote iTaukei language
item.description: For generations, knowledge has been passed down through talanoa, songs, and legends and now the iTaukei Trust Fund Board (TTFB) is turning that oral tradition into books for children. The board opened its inaugural Talanoa BookLab yesterday at the Centre for Appropriate Technology and Development in Nadave, where 12 to 15 authors will work with Ministry of Education’s curriculum advisers and illus
item.content:encoded:
For generations, knowledge has been passed down through talanoa, songs, and legends and now the iTaukei Trust Fund Board (TTFB) is turning that oral tradition into books for children.

The board opened its inaugural Talanoa BookLab yesterday at the Centre for Appropriate Technology and Development in Nadave, where 12 to 15 authors will work with Ministry of Education’s curriculum advisers and illustrators from August 31 to September 2.

The curriculum is aimed at students of Years 7 and 8.

The board’s senior program specialist, Unaisi Manulevu, said the project was about more than literacy.

“We are not only trying to preserve the language. We want the stories our children read to be culturally rooted and grounded and to help them understand who they are,” she said.

“We must go back to teaching our children not only to speak vosa vakaviti, but also to read it, write it and understand it.”

The initiative forms part of the board’s ongoing work to preserve and promote the iTaukei language and culture, and to ensure vosa vakaviti continues to be spoken, read, written and understood by future generations.

The stories will focus on themes such as climate change, nature, bula vaka vanua and vai tovo vaka vanua, helping young readers connect with their culture and environment.

Among those involved is illustrator Anare Somumu, who will guide the visual development of the stories on the final day.

After the workshop, the stories will go through the board’s publishing process before being printed as supplementary reading material.

item.title: Woman fined $200
item.description: A LABASA businesswoman has been fined $200 for dumping commercial waste into a public rubbish bin. Sky Tech Investment owner Shahimma Bi Khan pleaded guilty to one count of depositing commercial waste into a receptacle provided for public use, under the Litter Act 2008, when she appeared in the Labasa Magistrate’s Court.
item.content:encoded:
A LABASA businesswoman has been fined $200 for dumping commercial waste into a public rubbish bin.

Sky Tech Investment owner Shahimma Bi Khan pleaded guilty to one count of depositing commercial waste into a receptacle provided for public use, under the Litter Act 2008, when she appeared in the Labasa Magistrate’s Court.

The court heard that Ms Khan was seen at Nasekula, Labasa, on December 11, 2025, putting cartons and other rubbish from her business into a bin meant for public use.

Resident Magistrate Amelia Korodau said the rubbish came from Ms Khan’s business, and she was responsible for making sure her commercial waste was properly disposed of.

The court heard that Ms Khan, 34, is a sole trader and, therefore, responsible for providing the required facilities to manage waste from her business.

She was ordered to pay a $200 fine within 14 days, but would be jailed for 20 days if she failed to pay up.

The court noted that Ms Khan had no previous convictions, pleaded guilty at an early stage and was remorseful for the offence.

The maximum fine for an individual under the Act is $200, while a company can be fined up to $1000.

The court also warned Ms Khan that any further offence could result in a much higher fine.

item.title: Jail sentence for assaulting wife
item.description: A man was sentenced to seven months imprisonment for violently assaulting his wife after demanding money, meant for their sick baby’s hospital visit, to buy alcohol. The 34-year-old was convicted of assault after pleading guilty before Magistrate Samanunu Vaniqi.
item.content:encoded:
A man was sentenced to seven months imprisonment for violently assaulting his wife after demanding money, meant for their sick baby’s hospital visit, to buy alcohol.

The 34-year-old was convicted of assault after pleading guilty before Magistrate Samanunu Vaniqi.

The court heard that on June 11 this year, the man was drinking alcohol at home with friends when his wife informed him that their youngest child was sick. But the man, who was intoxicated at that time, demanded money to buy more alcohol.

After an argument ensued over prioritising alcohol over their sick child, his wife handed him $100 intended for taking their son to the hospital. He instead entered a vehicle with another individual.

When questioned by his wife, the man pushed her aside and repeatedly punched her. Upon returning home, he continued the assault by punching her, throwing her against a wall, choking her, and directing vulgar language at her.

The man was ordered to serve three months in jail, with the remaining four months suspended for three years.

The court also issued a final Domestic Violence Restraining Order (DVRO) to protect the complainant.
